title: Agur's Humble, Sharp Observations
overview: The sayings of Agur, an otherwise unknown wise man, move from a humble confession about God to a prayer for just enough and a string of numbered observations about people and nature.

parts.label: Agur admits his limits (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Agur appears nowhere else, and the Hebrew of verse 1 is so unclear that it may name his listeners, Ithiel and Ucal, or be a cry like "I am weary, God." He says he lacks wisdom, then asks who could climb to heaven or hold the wind in his fists, a challenge with only one possible answer: God.

parts.label: Trust and a prayer for enough (vv. 5-9)
parts.note: God's word is pictured as tested and pure like refined metal, a shelter that people should not pad with their own additions. Agur then asks for honesty and for neither poverty nor riches, since too much might make him forget God and too little might push him to steal.

parts.label: People who take and take (vv. 10-17)
parts.note: These lines describe people who slander, scorn their parents, think themselves clean and devour the poor, set beside things that are never satisfied, like a leech, the grave and fire. The blunt image of birds eating the eye of someone who mocks their parents points to a shameful end, perhaps a violent death, a body left unburied, or both.

parts.label: Hidden ways, upside down world (vv. 18-23)
parts.note: An eagle, a snake, a ship and a man with a young woman all leave no trail to follow, and the adulterous woman likewise wipes her mouth and claims innocence, though scholars debate exactly what links these lines. The next list reflects the rigid social order of its time, treating it as something the earth cannot bear when a servant becomes king, a despised woman marries, or a maid takes her mistress's place.

parts.label: Small creatures, proud walkers (vv. 24-31)
parts.note: Ants, rock dwelling animals called hyraxes, locusts and lizards succeed through planning, shelter, teamwork and boldness rather than strength. Then come things that move with confidence, ending with a king no one dares oppose, though the Hebrew for one animal is uncertain (perhaps a rooster or a greyhound).

parts.label: Stop before it escalates (vv. 32-33)
parts.note: If you have been arrogant or plotting harm, the advice is to put your hand over your mouth and stop. Just as churning milk makes butter and squeezing a nose draws blood, stirring up anger reliably produces a fight.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether verse 4's question about God's son is simply a poetic way of saying no human can match God, or a hint that some Christians read as pointing ahead to Jesus.
think: Agur asks for neither too little nor too much. What would "enough" look like in your own life, and how would you know when you had it?
